query: For high-value components operating in aggressive environments, what intervention could improve surface physical and mechanical characteristics? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence that would support it, and an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A post-deposition high-temperature annealing treatment that induces the in situ formation of a dense composite oxide layer (e.g., ZrTiO4) on high-entropy alloy (HEA) surfaces will enhance their surface mechanical and tribological properties in aggressive, high-temperature environments by providing a protective barrier against oxidation and wear.
generation.material_initial_state: Amorphous or as-deposited HEA film (e.g., AlCrTiZrMo HEA film) with no deliberately engineered surface oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Apply a thermal shock/annealing treatment by heating the HEA film at a high temperature for a prolonged duration in ambient air.
generation.conditions: High-temperature, oxidative, and tribocorrosive environments typical of high-value components in aggressive service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, stable composite oxide layer (e.g., ZrTiO4) that forms on the surface during annealing.
generation.mechanism: The high-temperature annealing promotes the controlled oxidation of specific elements in the HEA, whose sluggish diffusion due to multicomponent mixing facilitates the self-organized formation of a protective composite oxide film; this surface layer increases hardness, reduces friction, and enhances oxidation resistance by sealing the underlying metal from aggressive species.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated films, the annealed HEA films will exhibit lower coefficients of friction, reduced wear rates, and greater resistance against further high-temperature oxidation and tribocorrosion.
generation.baseline: HEA films in the as-deposited state without thermal treatment, which lack a deliberately formed protective oxide layer and thus show inferior surface mechanical performance in aggressive environments.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective as long as the operating temperatures, exposure to oxidizing conditions, and mechanical stresses remain within the range where the protective oxide layer remains stable. Its benefits might vary with different HEA compositions or under cyclic thermal/mechanical loading.
generation.uncertainty: While existing studies indicate improved tribocorrosion resistance after thermal shock treatments, uncertainties remain regarding the long-term stability of the oxide layer under cyclic conditions and its scalability across various HEA systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA films: one set will undergo the described thermal annealing (800°C for 1 hour in air) and the other will serve as an untreated control. Subject both groups to a standardized tribocorrosion test simulating high-temperature, oxidative, and mechanically aggressive conditions. Characterize the surface microstructure, oxide layer formation, and mechanical performance post-testing.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during sliding tests
Surface oxide layer composition and thickness (via XRD and microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally treated films do not show statistically significant improvements in friction, wear resistance, or demonstrate the presence of a dense, stable oxide layer compared to the untreated films, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

In marine engineering, the materials of mechanical components need to have service reliability in extremely harsh working environments, that is, on the basis of excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, they must also have the ability to resist the erosion of oxygen or corrosive media in high-temperature environments. The oxidation, friction and corrosion of the materials of power components are the process of chemical or electrochemical reactions between the materials and the medium in the surrounding environment, which leads to the failure of the materials. Therefore, the development of protective coatings and the study of the effect of thermal shock on the performance of protective coatings are particularly important.
